title: Fractions: Equal Parts of a Whole
subject: Mathematics
instructions: Use roti and paper-folding examples. Go slow on equal parts.

blocks.narration: Open by asking the class about sharing a roti.

data.text: Meena cuts one roti into 4 equal parts and eats one part. How much of the roti is left?

blocks.narration: Name the two numbers in a fraction.

data.heading: What a fraction tells us
paragraphs: When we break a whole thing into equal parts, each part is a fraction of the whole.
The number below the line is the denominator. It says how many equal parts the whole was broken into.
The number above the line is the numerator. It says how many of those parts we are talking about.

blocks.narration: Hop along the fourths from zero to one.

data.question: Tap each mark. Which mark lands on the same place as one half?

data.caption: Same numerator? The smaller denominator makes the bigger piece.

steps.title: Take a square of paper
steps.text: Any square sheet works. This is your whole.

steps.title: Fold it in half
steps.text: Both halves must match exactly when you press them together.

steps.title: Fold it in half again
steps.text: Open it out. You now see four equal squares.

steps.title: Shade one square
steps.text: The shaded part is one-fourth of the paper. Write 1/4 on it.

data.question: A chapati is torn into two pieces. One piece is much bigger. Is the small piece one-half?
options: Yes, because there are two pieces
No, because the two pieces are not equal
No, because a chapati cannot be halved
data.explanation: Half means the two pieces are exactly the same size. Unequal pieces are not halves.

data.title: Paper strip fraction hunt
instructions: Work in pairs. Each pair takes two paper strips of the same length.
Fold one strip into 2 equal parts and the other into 4 equal parts.
Shade 1 part of the first strip and 2 parts of the second strip.
Place the strips side by side. Are the shaded lengths the same?
Write what you found in one sentence.

blocks.narration: Two quick questions before the bell.

questions: Draw a circle cut into 4 equal parts and shade 3 of them. Write the fraction.
Which is bigger, 1/3 or 1/6? Say why in one sentence.

points: Many children say 1/6 is bigger than 1/3 because 6 is bigger. Use the paper strips, not words.
Insist on the word 'equal' every time a part is named.
If time runs short, move the paper strip hunt to homework.
